root.title: Do finer learned step sizes help a network learn? And does MetaOptimize beat a plain, well-tuned optimiser?
root.summary: The project began from two questions. First, does giving each part of a network its own learned step size, instead of one shared step size, help it learn? Second, does MetaOptimize, a method that learns its step size while training, beat a plain optimiser that is tuned well? The parts below are the ideas the project tested between 18 August and 28 September 2026.

parts.title: First look: do finer groups help?
parts.verdict: Helps with SGD+momentum, not AdamW; much of the gain was tuning
parts.summary: The question was whether giving different parts of the network their own learned step sizes beats one shared step size. With SGD plus momentum the finer groups looked clearly better, but with AdamW they did not. Most of the early gain turned out to be meta-step-size tuning, not finer groups.

leaves.title: Can the parent code run finer groups?
leaves.result: We wrote the missing code first
leaves.summary: The parent project's code never actually implemented the finer groupings (one step size per layer, per node, per weight), so the team wrote them first. It also fixed two defects (no data augmentation, and runs that could stop early without saying so) and passed its correctness tests.

leaves.title: Gate 0: 6 blocks vs one step size
leaves.result: SGDm +3.5 pp; AdamW tie; memory only
leaves.summary: The first check compared six step-size groups with a single shared step size. With SGD plus momentum, six groups won by 3.5 percentage points (91.5 vs 88.0 % accuracy); with AdamW the two tied, on only 2 seeds. This rests on notes written from memory, so it is not certain.
leaves.parentNote: Once finer groups could run, first asked if finer helps

leaves.title: Ladder: one per layer vs one overall
leaves.summary: Giving every layer its own step size beat one overall step size by 3.3 percentage points when both used the same meta step size. When each side got its own best meta step size, the gain shrank to 0.6. About 81-83 % of the apparent gain was really tuning.

leaves.title: Does the gain grow with bigger networks?
leaves.summary: The team asked whether the finer-group gain grows with bigger networks. It shrinks: +19.9, +2.9 and +0.9 points on ResNet-10, 18 and 34, because the single-step-size version stops failing in larger networks. ResNet-50 went the other way (-1.6 points), but with only 2 seeds.

leaves.title: Does the best grouping flip with longer training?
leaves.result: Flip was distance from each arm's best
leaves.summary: The best grouping seemed to flip as training got longer: per-node steps lost at 10 epochs and won at 40. But when each arm was given its own best meta step size, the lead faded smoothly to a tie. The flip measured distance from each arm's best setting, not the grouping.

parts.title: The adversarial review
parts.summary: Two days of adversarial review checked the early headline claims against the project's own control runs. Most were refuted: a cherry-picked best number, a 'robust' claim that was really a saturated dial, and scoring by the best epoch. New metric rules followed.

leaves.title: Early '+1.46 pp' headline
leaves.summary: The early headline gain of +1.46 percentage points was the best of 7 settings, each run with 3 seeds. The honest way to report it is the range across settings, +1.17 to +1.46.

leaves.title: 'Flat over 3 orders' robustness
leaves.result: Dial maxed out early; not robust
leaves.summary: The claim that the result was 'flat over three orders of magnitude' was not robustness. The pull dial saturated early: its half-life was at most 693 steps in a 50,000-step run, so every setting above 0.001 was fully saturated by the end.

leaves.title: Scoring by best epoch
leaves.summary: Scoring each run by its single best epoch inflates results by about 0.36 percentage points (median), as large as the effects being claimed. The project switched to the average of the last five epochs.

leaves.title: Pooling gain flips with training length
leaves.result: Refuted: on the right score nothing flips
leaves.summary: The claim that the pooling gain flips with training length (100 vs 300 epochs) was once called the strongest result in the project. It was measured on the wrong score and mixed up arm labels. On the right score nothing flips; gains only shrink.

leaves.title: How often did we correct ourselves?
leaves.summary: The project's record holds 28 self-corrections, 2 withdrawn headlines and 7 batches killed before using any GPU time (one list names only 6). Whether this process is worth writing up as a methods paper is not certain.

parts.title: The proposal: pull layer step sizes toward one
parts.verdict: Four kills; 'the project has no method left'
parts.summary: The proposal was to pull each layer's step size toward one shared value. Four separate experiments killed it, and a direct test of the proposal itself, plus a statistics-based version, also failed. Plain per-layer step sizes beat every partial pull, leaving the project with no method.

leaves.title: Kill 1: the pull dial r
leaves.result: Dial also cut step 10x; true pooling -3.0 pp
leaves.summary: The pull dial r also divided the meta step size by about 10, so it was not a pure pooling dial. A true full pooling, where all groups share one step size, lost 3.0 percentage points against plain per-layer step sizes. The earlier 'full pooling helps' claim was refuted.

leaves.title: Kill 2: tune the meta step size
leaves.result: Plain layerwise beats pooling by 0.4 pp
leaves.summary: Once the meta step size was tuned, plain per-layer step sizes (92.9 % accuracy) beat the best pooled version (92.4 %) by 0.4 percentage points. Pooling cost accuracy and added another setting to tune.

leaves.title: Kill 3: start from a sane step size
leaves.result: 76 % of the gain was a crippled start
leaves.summary: Starting from a sane step size (1e-3 instead of a crippled 1e-6) removed 76 % of the apparent gain from partial pooling. The gain fell from +1.0 to +0.24 points, below the project's own 0.5-point bar for mattering.

leaves.title: Kill 4: other networks, CIFAR-100
leaves.result: No sweet spot; full pooling falls to 9 %
leaves.summary: The sweet spot did not carry over to other networks (ResNet-10, ResNet-34) or to CIFAR-100. On CIFAR-100 with a sane starting step size the curve ran straight to the end with no sweet spot, and full pooling collapsed to 9 %.

leaves.title: The proposal itself
leaves.result: Plain layerwise beats every partial pull
leaves.summary: The two-level proposal itself (a shared step size plus a small per-group offset) was tested directly in 42 runs. Its best setting trailed plain per-layer step sizes by 0.25 points at one start and 0.82 at the other. Every partial pull lost.

leaves.title: Statistics-based pull
leaves.summary: A statistics-based way of choosing the pull strength (empirical-Bayes, James-Stein style) was tried to save the idea without tuning a dial. It lifted accuracy by only 0.04 points; the pre-set bar for success was 1.16.

parts.title: Reading the learned signal; Ideas 1-3
parts.verdict: Two ideas dead; Idea 3 (steady across step sizes) survives; the signal is a diagnostic, not a method
parts.summary: With no method left, the team studied the learned signal itself and tried three ideas. Ideas 1 and 2 died; Idea 3, staying steady across starting step sizes, survived. The signal turned out to be a diagnostic, not a method.

leaves.title: Does noise average down as expected?
leaves.result: No: far slower than the theory says
leaves.summary: Averaging over more weights is supposed to cut noise as one over the square root of the group size. The measured slopes were far shallower, between -0.09 and -0.38 against the -0.5 that theory needs, so noise averages down much more slowly than assumed.

leaves.title: Our '53 % sign agreement' claim
leaves.result: Refuted: sat below its own floor
leaves.summary: The project's claim that 53 % of per-weight signals agree in sign was refuted. It mixed two arms; the 53.1 % figure belongs to the 62-group arm, whose chance level is 55.1 %, so it actually sat 1.9 points below that floor.

leaves.title: Does adapting create shared structure?
leaves.result: Yes: free step sizes create it
leaves.summary: Does adapting the step sizes create shared structure? Yes: the fraction of independent information the groups carried was 0.16 to 0.55 with free step sizes, against 0.03 to 0.08 when they were frozen. So the free step sizes themselves create the structure.

leaves.title: Choose groups from that structure
leaves.result: Signal and best grouping never match: 0 of 21
leaves.summary: The idea was to pick step-size groups at the scale where the signal has structure. It never matched: the signal peaks at a very different scale from the best-accuracy grouping, by at least 512 times, and the match test fired in 0 of 21 cases.

leaves.title: Idea 1: steer step size toward cosine schedule
leaves.summary: Idea 1 steered the learned step size toward a cosine schedule. Its best arm scored 92.5 %, 1.9 percentage points below a tuned baseline, so it was stopped by its own pre-set rule. A small real effect exists, but the exact schedule behind it was not saved.

leaves.title: Idea 2: pick groups from correlation
leaves.summary: Idea 2 chose step-size groups from the measured correlation between layers. The extra same-sign agreement was +0.0001 points (kill line: 0.1), so the signal the idea needed is not there. The idea was dropped.

leaves.title: Idea 3: forgiving of a bad start
leaves.summary: Idea 3 asks whether MetaOptimize forgives a badly chosen start. It stays steady over a 100,000-fold range of starting step sizes, where a fixed rate collapses, at a price of about 1.1 percentage points below its own best setting. So it is forgiving, but it does not win.

leaves.title: Direction C: signal predicts accuracy
leaves.result: Failed its own test written in advance
leaves.summary: Direction C bet that the signal could predict accuracy. Its own test, written in advance, said otherwise: where accuracy rose 0.73 points the signal fell, and where the signal moved a lot accuracy did not move. Direction C was dropped.

parts.title: The count-matched audit
parts.verdict: Effect holds in 20 of 20 cells (decay 0.1); no explanation survived
parts.summary: Holding the number of step-size groups equal, does it matter which weights share a group? Equal-sized chunks beat groups that follow the network's structure in 20 of 20 cells, all at weight decay 0.1. Yet no explanation survived: the effect tracks group sizes, and every other candidate cause failed.

leaves.title: Same count, which cut? Chunks vs nodewise
leaves.summary: Two ways of cutting the network into about 14,400 step-size groups were compared at the same group count: equal-sized chunks versus one group per output channel (following the architecture), in one batch. Chunks won by +0.49 percentage points, about three times the noise. So granularity is two things: how many groups, and which weights share one.
leaves.keyReason: Headline: the count-matched audit, about 3× its noise.

leaves.title: Does it hold in every cell?
leaves.summary: The chunks-versus-aligned comparison was repeated across datasets, networks and optimisers. Chunks came out ahead in all 20 count-matched cells (at least three times the noise in 18), with gains from +0.14 to +1.64 points. All 20 ran at weight decay 0.1, a strong setting.
leaves.keyReason: Headline: the count-matched audit, positive in 20 of 20 cells.

leaves.title: Alignment: do groups follow the network?
leaves.result: No effect seen; not ruled out (not certain)
leaves.summary: Does the effect come from groups following the network's structure? Shuffling which weights sit in which group, with the same count and the same sizes, changed accuracy by about zero: -0.009 points, and -0.018 when repeated at twice the power. This is a limited null, not proof that alignment never matters; a moderate effect could have been missed, so it is not certain.
leaves.parentNote: Confirmed effect raised: which property of the partition carries it?

leaves.title: Group sizes carry the effect
leaves.result: Sizes alone recover the whole gap
leaves.summary: In the shuffle test, changing only the group sizes (equal chunks instead of the aligned sizes) gave +0.590 points, about 101.6 % of the whole effect; alignment added nothing. In the aligned grouping, 66.64 % of the groups hold a single weight, yet those cover only 0.09 % of the weights. So the spread of group sizes carries the effect.
leaves.parentNote: Same question, answered by the size-distribution arm of pp1
leaves.keyReason: Headline: the count-matched audit, group sizes alone carry the effect.

leaves.title: The size-1 tail as a general law
leaves.result: Killed by four checks on stored data
leaves.summary: It was suggested that the effect comes from the many one-weight groups, as a general rule about group sizes. Four checks on data already stored killed that: for example, removing every one-weight group bought nothing (+0.115 points, within noise). What survives is narrower: splitting the 41 one-dimensional normalisation tensors into single weights costs accuracy.

leaves.title: Is it specific to BatchNorm?
leaves.summary: Is the effect specific to BatchNorm, a layer type that normalises using batch statistics? The same comparison on a GroupNorm network, which uses no batch statistics, also showed the effect. So BatchNorm is not required, which removes one candidate explanation.

leaves.title: Caused by Adam-style rescaling?
leaves.result: Refuted: AdamW-base run still shows it
leaves.summary: Might the effect come from Adam-style rescaling, where updates are divided by a running size of recent gradients? A run with AdamW as the base optimiser and RMSProp, another rescaler, as the step-size learner still showed the effect (+0.889 points, above the +0.55 bar set in advance). So a rescaling step anywhere in the loop does not explain it.

leaves.title: A count slope to carry between settings
leaves.summary: Could one count slope (accuracy change per tenfold change in group count) be carried between settings to correct comparisons whose counts differ? The four available slopes spread by 0.129 points per tenfold against a 0.10 bar, and in one batch the sign changed with training length. So no stable slope exists.

leaves.title: Twenty statistics of the group sizes
leaves.result: None explained what drives the effect
leaves.summary: Twenty candidate statistics of the list of group sizes, such as the share of one-weight groups, were checked to see which one carries the effect. With only three arms in the design, at most two statistics can be told apart, so none could be identified, and one apparent best predictor was the three-arm test in disguise. Which property of the sizes matters is still open.

leaves.title: Predict the effect from any setting
leaves.summary: Can the size of the effect be predicted from a measurable property of a setting, such as accuracy level, group count or dataset? The best predictor seemed to cut the error by 18 %, but all of that came from a single CIFAR-100 point, and on the ten CIFAR-10 folds the plain average did better. So no prediction works.

leaves.title: Does the base optimiser change it?
leaves.summary: The effect looked larger under some base optimisers: SGD +1.000, RMSProp +0.720, SGD with momentum +0.556, AdamW +0.189 points. But once the batch each came from is accounted for, the difference is not clear (p = 0.128), so the word 'identified' was withdrawn. The base optimiser stays a candidate explanation, not a confirmed one.

parts.title: The denominator: vs a plain tuned optimiser
parts.summary: Does MetaOptimize beat a plain, well-tuned optimiser? No: against tuned SGD with momentum and a cosine schedule it loses by 1.8 percentage points on CIFAR-10 and by up to 14.6 on CIFAR-100. The audit's own effect (about +0.56 points) is roughly ten times smaller than this deficit.

leaves.title: Is our plain-SGD baseline trustworthy?
leaves.summary: Before comparing, the plain-SGD baseline was checked: does our training code reproduce a known good result? Tuned SGD with momentum and a cosine schedule reached 94.766 % on CIFAR-10, inside the 94.5-95.5 % band written down in advance. So the later gaps belong to the method, not to buggy code.

leaves.title: CIFAR-10, tuned SGD + cosine
leaves.summary: On CIFAR-10, MetaOptimize was compared with plain SGD tuned and run with a cosine schedule. It came out behind by 1.8 percentage points (headline value 1.796). The best single MetaOptimize arm scored 93.304 %, 1.461 behind the 94.766 % baseline; the figures compare slightly different pairs.
leaves.keyReason: Supporting: tuned plain SGD beats MetaOptimize (1.8 pp).

leaves.title: Does longer training close the gap?
leaves.summary: Does training much longer close the gap? Matched on configuration, the CIFAR-10 deficit was 1.82, 1.97 and 1.94 points at 100, 300 and 600 epochs (passes over the training images). It neither widens nor closes, so a longer horizon is no defence for the method.
leaves.keyReason: Supporting: the gap stays flat with longer training (about 1.9 pp).

leaves.title: CIFAR-100
leaves.result: Behind 5.7 pp; plain SGD wins every rung
leaves.summary: On CIFAR-100, a plain SGD ladder of six learning rates was run beside MetaOptimize in one batch. The best rung beat MetaOptimize by 5.70 percentage points (about 19 times the noise), and every rung won, the smallest margin being 3.48 points. Plain SGD at 200 epochs reached 78.83 %.
leaves.keyReason: Supporting: plain SGD wins every rung (5.7 pp).

leaves.title: Parent paper's setting (no augmentation)
leaves.summary: The comparison was repeated in the parent paper's own setting, without data augmentation (random flips and crops of the training images). Tuned plain SGD still won: by 3.62 points on CIFAR-10 and 12.18 on CIFAR-100. Against the parent's own 6-block set-up on CIFAR-10 the gap was 15.12 points.
leaves.keyReason: Supporting: the gap in the parent's setting (3.6 pp and 12.2 pp).

leaves.title: Fair decay? CIFAR-100 at 5e-4
leaves.summary: The first CIFAR-100 comparison ran MetaOptimize at a strong step-size-scaled weight decay (0.1). Re-running it at the standard 5e-4 did not help: the deficit grew from 5.71 to 14.59 points (about 45 times the noise). Moving to the standard decay does not rescue the method against the plain baseline.
leaves.keyReason: Supporting: the gap widens to 14.6 pp.

parts.title: Where the CIFAR-100 collapse lives
parts.verdict: Located in three tensors by vote size; 'This is not a mechanism'
parts.summary: On CIFAR-100, one shared step size reached only about 23 % accuracy while one per layer reached about 70 %. Step by step the collapse was narrowed to three BatchNorm scales, 0.014 % of the weights, and giving them their own step sizes recovers the whole gap. The project's own verdict is that this locates the collapse by size of vote and is not a mechanism.

leaves.title: Is it the last layers (the head)?
leaves.summary: Is the collapse in the last layers, the head? Giving the head its own step size recovered only about 4 % of the 46.9-point gap, less than an arbitrary split in the middle (about 22 %). So the head is not where it lives.

leaves.title: Which single tensor is the cliff?
leaves.summary: Sweeping where a two-group cut falls, the best position was 49. Stepping one tensor at a time around it, moving a single BatchNorm scale of just 512 numbers was worth +24.8 percentage points, while neighbouring steps, one moving 131,072 parameters, gave no such gain. So it is not about how much of the network moves.
leaves.parentNote: Head test failed and started the cut-position line

leaves.title: Real, or a 100-epoch artefact?
leaves.summary: Is the cliff an artefact of stopping at 100 epochs? Training for 772 epochs, over seven times longer, the cliff survived but shrank (to 19.34 points, 5.67 smaller). The best cut position also stayed at 49 on fresh seeds.
leaves.parentNote: Asks whether the cliff is only a 100-epoch effect

leaves.title: Position, list order or mass?
leaves.summary: Is it a tensor's identity, its position in the list, contiguity, or mass? Matching total mass exactly (3,956,288 parameters) did not reproduce the effect, so coarse mass is refuted. The list-order test could not decide between identity and position because its planned outcome was unreachable, so that part stays unresolved.

leaves.title: Which tensors carry the vote?
leaves.summary: A probe logged each tensor's contribution to the shared signal that steers the step size, so each tensor 'votes' it up or down. Three BatchNorm scales of 512 numbers each, 0.014 % of the weights, carried the sign against the other 59 tensors and voted the step size down on every pinned record. This is the clearest single measurement of the project.
leaves.keyReason: Case study: the collapse traced to 3 BatchNorm scales.

leaves.title: Lift them out: is it causal?
leaves.summary: Causal test: give the three carrier tensors their own step sizes while the other 59 keep sharing one. Accuracy rose from 23.28 % to 70.21 %, +46.9 points, the whole gap and no better than one step size per layer. Giving a matched set of look-alike tensors their own step sizes did nothing (-0.06 points).
leaves.keyReason: Case study: lifting the 3 scales out recovers the whole gap.

leaves.title: Would any three tensors at that depth do?
leaves.summary: Would any three similar BatchNorm tensors at that depth do? A matched trio of non-carriers recovered only 0.36 % of the gap (+0.17 points), while isolating the real carriers beat it by 46.5 points. So these tensors matter, though a later test asked whether their identity or the size of their vote is the cause.
leaves.parentNote: Obvious objection to the rescue: would any matched trio do?
leaves.keyReason: Case study: a matched trio of other scales does not.

leaves.title: Does it exist beyond ResNet?
leaves.summary: Does the gap exist beyond ResNet-18? On VGG11, a plain BatchNorm network with no residual connections, the gap was +31.3 points and isolating one nominated tensor rescued +31.3. It also appeared on a GroupNorm version and on PlainNet18, so it is not specific to one network.
leaves.keyReason: Case study: the same on VGG, GroupNorm and PlainNet.

leaves.title: Tensor identity or size of vote?
leaves.summary: Is the rescue about which tensors they are, or how big their vote is? The carriers' summed contribution was 308 times a matched control's, and they rank 1 to 3 of 62. The test design cannot separate identity from size of vote on this network. The project's own words: 'This is not a mechanism.'

leaves.title: Silence the vote, or force the step?
leaves.summary: Lifting a carrier out changes two things: its vote leaves the shared sum, and it gets its own step size. On PlainNet, silencing the vote alone did not rescue. A clean separation showed both matter, +15.4 points from the vote and +37.8 from the applied step, so the applied step matters more.
leaves.parentNote: Isolation changes two things at once; which one matters?

leaves.title: On CIFAR-10, does the vote-size story hold?
leaves.result: Yes: key tensors biggest, never win vote
leaves.summary: Do the same three tensors dominate on CIFAR-10, where nothing collapses? They are still the largest single contributors, but they fix the shared sign on 0 of 1,500 records, against 0.8069 on the collapsing CIFAR-100 case. They never out-vote the other 59 tensors there, which fits the size-of-vote story.

parts.title: Is the collapse a real hazard?
parts.verdict: A corner case, not a general hazard
parts.summary: This part asked whether the collapse, where training with one shared step size stalls at low accuracy, is a real hazard. It turned out to need a weight decay near 0.1; at the standard 5e-4, or with a standard AdamW recipe, it does not appear. So it is a corner case, not a general hazard.

leaves.title: Needs momentum 0.99, or weight decay?
leaves.result: Decay is needed; momentum is not
leaves.summary: Two settings were changed one at a time. With momentum lowered from 0.99 to 0.9 the collapse still happened (a gap of 44.8 points stayed); with weight decay removed it went away and the shared step size gained 48.8 points. So decay is needed here; momentum is not.

leaves.title: Switch decay off on all 20 scales
leaves.summary: Weight decay was switched off on all 20 normalisation scales (4,800 of 11.2 million parameters). The collapse vanished: the shared-step-size arm rose from 22.95 to 70.78 percent, a gain of 47.8 points. This was run at the campaign's weight decay of 0.1.

leaves.title: Switch decay off on just the 3 key scales
leaves.result: +47.3 pp: three do the work of twenty
leaves.summary: Decay was switched off on only the three scales that dominate the shared step-size vote (1,536 of about 11.2 million parameters). The shared-step-size arm recovered by 47.3 points, inside the recovery band of the all-20 arm. So three tensors do as much as all twenty.
leaves.parentNote: All-20 mask could not say which tensors carried it
leaves.keyReason: Case study: switching decay off on just the 3 scales recovers the gap.

leaves.title: Is one carrier enough?
leaves.summary: The question was whether one of the three key scales is enough, or whether only the count matters. At a matched count of two, the carrier pair recovered (67.1 percent) while a carrier-free pair stayed at the floor (22.9). A single carrier recovered part of the way, a gain of 35.8 points.
leaves.parentNote: Control triple left a count/dose rival alive

leaves.title: Is it there at normal decay 5e-4?
leaves.result: No: one step size ahead by 4.5 pp
leaves.summary: The collapse was tested at four weight decays. At 0.1 the per-layer arm led by 46.1 points, but at the standard 5e-4 the one-step-size arm was ahead by 4.5 points, so the ordering reversed. The collapse does not appear at normal decay, which turned the campaign's story into a corner case.

leaves.title: Standard recipe: AdamW base + Adam meta
leaves.result: No collapse; the pre-set test said no
leaves.summary: With the standard recipe (AdamW base, Adam meta optimiser) nothing collapsed: the one-step-size arm was 5.1 points ahead, and the pre-set test said to stop. Not certain why: that run also had about 50 times lower realised decay dose, so the base optimiser cannot be credited alone.

leaves.title: Which decay route carries it?
leaves.result: Shrinking the weights alone is enough (+47.3 pp)
leaves.summary: Three variants separated how decay acts. Keeping the weight shrink that follows the learned step size gave the collapse (+47.3 points); keeping only the memory term gave no gap, and a fixed-rate decay gave no gap. So the weight-shrink route is enough; it was not shown to be required.

leaves.title: Is that route required (necessity)?
leaves.summary: The earlier test showed that the weight-shrink route is enough to cause the collapse. It did not show that any route is required, and the shrink-only arm still kept one decay term undecayed inside the memory. So whether the route is necessary is still open.

leaves.title: Rival: short-horizon bias
leaves.result: Excluded as a sufficient cause (a bound)
leaves.summary: A rival explanation was short-horizon bias (picking too-small step sizes because the meta-learner looks only a short way ahead). With the decay removed and the horizon shortened directly, nothing collapsed; the one-step-size arm stayed 3.7 to 5.6 points ahead in all three cells. Excluded as a sufficient cause only, a bound.

leaves.title: Does vote capture come first?
leaves.summary: The idea was that a few big contributors first capture the shared step-size vote, and only then does accuracy fall. In 498 earlier probe runs the accuracy gap opened 700 to 1,700 steps before the learned step size turned, on 15 of 15 pairs. So capture comes after the damage, not before.

leaves.title: Early warning from the first epochs
leaves.summary: A measure taken in the first epochs was meant to warn which runs would collapse. It did not separate collapsing runs from healthy ones: the best cut still got 47 of 171 runs wrong, while simply guessing the commoner outcome gets 53 wrong. So the early warning does not work.

parts.title: Stress tests of the audit
parts.verdict: Sign kept at 0.1; size at standard decay undecided; one-step-size row open
parts.summary: This part asked whether the count-matched audit (the finding that a uniform split of step sizes beats an architecture-aligned split) survives stress tests. The sign holds at weight decay 0.1 and 0.01. Its size at the standard decay is undecided, and the one-step-size row is still open.

leaves.title: Audit at three weight decays
leaves.summary: The audit's key comparison was repeated at three weight decays. The lead of the uniform split over the aligned one held at 0.1 (+0.37 points) and at 0.01 (+0.45). At the standard 5e-4 it was +0.24 with a range of -0.01 to +0.49, so it is undecided.

leaves.title: One step size vs groups, standard decay, untuned
leaves.summary: At the standard decay 5e-4, with no re-tuning, a plain single step size beat both audited groupings by 2.6 and 2.8 points. That looked like a problem for the audit, but it was later superseded: re-tuning each grouping closed most of the lead.

leaves.title: Re-tune each grouping
leaves.result: Shrank to a tie; superseded by wider re-tune
leaves.summary: Each grouping was re-tuned at 5e-4 over four settings, chosen on training accuracy. The single step size's lead shrank to +0.45 and +0.69 points, then to a tie once a bias allowance was subtracted (a bound, not equality). Every grouping chose the edge of its grid, so a wider re-tune followed.
leaves.parentNote: Checked whether scalar's lead was a tuning artefact

leaves.title: Re-tune past the grid edge
leaves.summary: The re-tune was run again with the search extended past the earlier edge (45 runs), but nothing was located: every grouping still picked a grid edge. The tuned gap was -0.04 and -0.14 points, within a range of -0.72 to +0.44, so it is undecided, and unresolved is not a tie.
leaves.parentNote: Re-tune had hit grid edge, so axis extended

leaves.title: Check on held-out images
leaves.result: Rankings unresolved; both pick same settings
leaves.summary: The audit's rankings, reported on test accuracy, were re-read on 5,000 held-out training images. The test and validation readings differ on the key comparison, so the rankings are unresolved; the single step size still beat the best grouping on both. Both pick the same settings.

leaves.title: Audit on CIFAR-100
leaves.result: Holds at 0.1; no reading at standard decay
leaves.summary: The audit was repeated on CIFAR-100, a second dataset. At weight decay 0.1 it holds (+1.22 points). At the standard 5e-4 there is no reading, because one grouping hit the upper limit of its step-size range on all four seeds, so neither a survive nor a vanish statement is allowed.

leaves.title: Fixed-rate decay at the audit setting
leaves.summary: The audit was run with a fixed-rate decay that does not follow the learned step size, at two rates. Neither run could be read: one hit the upper limit of its step-size range, and in the other every arm stayed below the 85 percent health bar. The headline is neither confirmed nor removed.

parts.title: Which paper? (21-22 Sep)
parts.verdict: ICML paper closed; one paper for TMLR
parts.summary: This part laid out four candidate papers and ran a pre-set test to decide between them. The one about vote capture was closed by its own test, and one was merged into another. A single paper was chosen, the count-matched audit for the journal TMLR.

leaves.title: C1 'vote capture': the ICML paper
leaves.result: Closed by its own gate; ICML under 5 %
leaves.summary: The first candidate paper claimed a few scales capture the shared step-size vote and cause the collapse. Its own pre-set gate said to stop if the standard recipe did not collapse, and it did not. So it was closed, and the chance at the ICML conference was put under 5 percent (a judgement).

leaves.title: C2 'decay decides granularity'
leaves.result: Merged into the audit paper as a section
leaves.summary: The second candidate said decay decides which step-size grouping wins: without the collapse, one step size does as well as finer groups. The finer grouping wins only in the collapse at decay 0.1, because the single step size is broken there. It was merged into the audit paper as a section.
leaves.keyReason: Decay decides granularity, merged into the audit paper as a section.

leaves.title: C3 parent's advantage depends on decay
leaves.summary: The third candidate claimed the parent paper's advantage at its own setting depends on decay: present at 0.1, absent at 0.01 or below. This was unsupported and partly contradicted by the data. The supervisor decides whether to act on it.

leaves.title: C4 count-matched audit: the one paper
leaves.result: Chosen for TMLR; 60-70 % chance is a judgement
leaves.summary: The fourth candidate was the existing count-matched audit: at the same group count, a uniform split beat an architecture-aligned one in 20 of 20 cells (about +0.56 points), and MetaOptimize lost to tuned SGD with cosine. It was chosen as the one paper, for TMLR. The 60-70 percent acceptance chance is a judgement, not a measurement.

parts.title: Planned but never run
parts.dates: state at 28 Sep; nothing found since
parts.summary: This part lists experiments that were planned but never run. As of 28 Sep the record shows three ranked next steps and older plan rows, none registered, and nothing was found after that date (not certain). None of the top three was needed for the TMLR paper.

leaves.title: Extend the re-tune grid upward
leaves.summary: This planned test would extend the re-tune grid upward (three groupings, two larger meta step sizes, three seeds, 18 runs). It would show whether either grouping's best setting finally lands inside the grid. It was never run; cost about 16 GPU-hours (an estimate).

leaves.title: Re-tune with a validation split
leaves.summary: This planned test would repeat the last re-tune but pick settings on 5,000 held-out images instead of training accuracy (45 runs). It would show whether held-out selection picks the same settings. It was never run; cost about 39 GPU-hours (an estimate).

leaves.title: Raised-ceiling probe
leaves.summary: This planned diagnostic would raise the ceiling on the starting step size to 0.3 (9 runs) to see whether the single step size's chosen setting is a real best point or just the old ceiling. Its result could not be compared with earlier batches. Never run; about 8 GPU-hours (an estimate).

leaves.title: Exempt 1-D tensors from weight decay
leaves.summary: This planned test would leave all one-dimensional tensors (biases and normalisation scales) without weight decay, as the standard recipe does. It would show whether the collapse still exists at decay 0.1. Never run; 12 runs, about 8.4 GPU-hours (an estimate).

leaves.title: Seven other planned rows (ViT, toy model ...)
leaves.result: Never run; no transformer, no theory
leaves.summary: Seven further rows from the older plan were never run: locating the decay transition, replicating on other networks, a magnitude-versus-identity test, more seeds, a small ViT, Tiny-ImageNet and a toy model. So there is no transformer result and no theory.
